learn: The software development life cycle (SDLC), the roles in a software team and how development evolved from waterfall to cloud-native and AI-assisted (ADLC)
How data science evolved, what it is, and how it overlaps with AI and ML
Data roles (data engineer, data scientist, ML engineer) and the data science hierarchy of needs
ML basics: AI ⊃ ML ⊃ deep learning ⊃ LLMs/GenAI, training vs inference, and the three axes of change (code, data, model)
The ML modelling cycle and the five-step model workflow
Three generations of ML, ML domains (language, speech, vision, decision) and foundation models
The AI engineer role and why specifying ML behaviour differs from specifying ordinary software
intro.why: Software engineering for ML starts from one observation: a model is a small part of a larger software system that has to be specified, built, tested, deployed and maintained by a team. Everything later in this subject (requirements, architecture, code quality, testing, deployment, responsible AI) builds on the vocabulary introduced here.
prereq: Basic idea of supervised learning (inputs, labels, predictions)
Some exposure to how software is built in teams

symbols: Model Context Protocol (standard way to connect models to tools)

sections.title: The software development life cycle and its roles
sections.plain: Plan → analyse → design → build → test → deploy → maintain, done by a team of specialists.
sections.body:
The SDLC is a structured process to plan, build, test, deploy and maintain software. It is usually drawn as a loop because maintenance feeds new requirements back into planning:

Planning → Analysis → Design → Development → Testing → Deployment → Maintenance → (back to planning)

RoleResponsibility
Business analystTranslates business needs into clear technical requirements
Project managerPlans, coordinates and tracks execution to meet deadlines
Product ownerDefines the product vision and prioritises features for value
Team leadGuides the team technically and keeps tasks moving
QA teamValidates quality through systematic testing, ideally shift-left (testing early)
Scrum masterFacilitates agile processes and removes impediments
DevelopersImplement the functionality
Software architectDesigns the overall structure and technical strategy
UX/UI designersDesign intuitive, user-friendly interfaces
TestersFind defects and verify the software meets requirements

ML projects keep all of these roles and add data and ML roles (next sections). The SDLC does not disappear when ML arrives; it gains new loops for data and models.

sections.title: From waterfall to cloud-native and AI-assisted development
sections.plain: Process, architecture, deployment and infrastructure all evolved together.
sections.body:
EraDevelopment processApplication architectureDeployment and packagingInfrastructure
≈1980WaterfallMonolithicPhysical serverDatacenter
≈2000AgileN-tierVirtual serversHosted
≈2010DevOpsMicroservicesContainersCloud

Cloud-native application = agile + DevOps + microservices + containers + cloud.

The next step, sometimes called moving from SDLC to ADLC, infuses AI into scaled agile delivery:

ModelStrengthWeakness
WaterfallPredictable phasesStatic documents, defects found late, long time to market
IterativeEvolving documents, continuous testingKeeping documents in sync; overhead
AgileJust-enough documentation, CI/CDDepends heavily on people's skills and robust automation
Scaled agileConsistency across many teamsCoordination effort
Scaled agile + AI (ADLC)AI assists with documents, code, tests and deployment scripts: faster time to market, less dependence on individuals, more consistent qualityRequires governance of AI-generated artefacts

sections.title: Data science: evolution, definitions and convergence
sections.plain: From files to intelligent systems; data science turns data into decisions.
sections.body:
How data handling evolved: 1960s files and spreadsheets → 1970 relational databases (Codd) → 1989 knowledge discovery in databases (KDD) → early 2000s data warehousing, ETL and business intelligence → mid-2000s social media and unstructured data → 2006–08 cloud computing (AWS, Azure) → 2010–15 big data (Hadoop) → 2017–18 Transformer models (the architecture was published in 2017; BERT and GPT followed in 2018). The trend: from manual data capture to intelligent systems.

Definitions of data science: the study of data; the art of uncovering insights and trends hidden in data; translating data into a story whose insights support decisions; and, broadly, every stage from collection and preprocessing through analysis, prediction and visualisation.

Convergence: data science sits at the overlap of mathematics and statistics, computer science/IT and domain knowledge. Maths + CS gives machine learning; CS + domain gives software development; maths + domain gives traditional research. AI, data science and ML overlap rather than nest neatly.

sections.title: Data roles: engineer, scientist, ML engineer
sections.plain: Data engineers move data, data scientists find insight, ML engineers run models in production.
sections.body:
RoleTypical flowOutput
Data engineerSources → ETL pipelines → data warehouse → BIReliable, queryable data
Data scientistData → exploration → model → (often one-time) forecast or insightModels, analyses, decisions
ML engineerClient data → model in production → predictions; ground truth collected; monitoring and analysis; additional data fed backRunning, monitored ML services

The ML engineer's loop is what makes ML engineering: predictions go out, ground truth comes back, performance is monitored, and new data is used to improve the model. Team structures vary (centralised, embedded, hybrid), but these responsibilities appear in every mature team.

sections.title: The data science hierarchy of needs
sections.plain: Collect → move/store → explore/transform → aggregate/label → learn/optimise → AI.
sections.body:
Like Maslow's pyramid, each level needs the ones below it:

  1. Collect: instrumentation, logging, sensors, external data, user-generated content (data infrastructure engineers).
  2. Move/store: reliable data flow, infrastructure, pipelines, ETL, structured and unstructured storage (data engineers).
  3. Explore/transform: cleaning, anomaly detection, preparation.
  4. Aggregate/label: analytics, metrics, segments, aggregates, features, training data (data scientists/analysts).
  5. Learn/optimise: A/B testing, experimentation, simple ML algorithms.
  6. AI, deep learning (ML engineers).

The engineering lesson: most of the work, and most failures, sit in the lower levels. A team that jumps to deep learning without reliable collection, storage and cleaning builds on sand.

sections.title: What machine learning is, and why it is harder to engineer
sections.plain: ML learns rules from data; three things change instead of one.
sections.body:
Machine learning is the branch of AI that uses data and algorithms to imitate the way humans learn, gradually improving accuracy. Nesting: AI ⊃ ML ⊃ deep learning ⊃ {large language models, generative AI}.

Three axes of change. In ordinary software only the code changes. In ML three things change, each for its own reasons:

AxisWhy it changes
DataSchema changes, sampling over time, volume
ModelNew algorithms, more training, experiments
CodeBusiness needs, bug fixes, configuration

Any combination can change at once ($2^3-1=7$ non-empty combinations vs 1 for plain software), so testing, versioning and deployment must track all three together (continuous delivery for ML).

Model: the trained algorithm used to make predictions; the core of an ML system that is developed, deployed, monitored and maintained in a pipeline. Training: historical data → learning algorithm → model. Inference (testing/serving): new data → model → predictions.

sections.title: The ML modelling cycle and the model workflow
sections.plain: Manage data → train → evaluate → deploy → monitor → retrain, around and around.
sections.body:
Modelling cycle: (1) manage data: collect, explore, cleanse, prepare, split; (2) train: pick the task, engineer features, select algorithms; (3) evaluate: score, assess, compare; (4) deploy: apply to fresh data, monitor outcomes, improve; then update with new data and repeat.

Model workflow (five steps)
  1. Development: build and train using training data (algorithm choice, hyperparameter tuning, evaluation).
  2. Versioning: track model versions as they improve or adapt to new data.
  3. Deployment: put the trained model into production to predict on live data.
  4. Monitoring: watch live performance for data drift, degradation and bias.
  5. Retraining: update the model periodically with new data to maintain performance.

sections.title: Three generations of ML
sections.plain: Train small models → retrain deep models on big data → call pre-trained models through APIs.
sections.body:
GenerationEnablerTypical effort
1. Basic MLLabelled datasets, classical algorithmsCreate labelled data, train, measure performance
2. Deep learningArtificial neural networks, big dataRetrain with DL algorithms, measure performance
3. Transfer learning / TransformersPre-trained and fine-tuned modelsUse models through APIs, often pay-per-use; little or no training

The engineering consequence: in generation 3, much of the work moves from training models to integrating, evaluating and operating someone else's model inside your system.

sections.title: ML domains: language, speech, vision and decisions
sections.plain: Cloud AI services are grouped into language, speech, vision and decision services.
sections.body:
Service familyWhat it provides
LanguageNLP for understanding and analysing text
SpeechSpeech-to-text, text-to-speech, speech translation, speaker recognition
Computer visionImage and video recognition
DecisionRecommendations for informed, efficient decisions

NLP tasks built on Transformers: text classification, summarisation, question answering, named-entity recognition, language modelling, text generation, translation.

Computer vision tasks: object detection (surveillance, robotics), face recognition (unlocking devices, security), feature extraction, image classification, image restoration (inpainting, deblurring, pixel interpolation, denoising).

Automatic speech recognition (ASR) converts spoken language into text in real time or from recordings; used in virtual assistants, transcription and call centres.

Humanoid robots such as Sophia combine several of these domains (vision, speech, language) in one system, which is exactly the integration challenge this subject is about.

sections.title: Foundation models, LLMs and the AI engineer
sections.plain: Big pre-trained models adapted to many tasks; a new engineering role builds with them.
sections.body:
Foundation models are large models trained on broad data and adaptable to many tasks with little task-specific tuning (through fine-tuning or other transfer learning). Large language models are deep models that recognise, extract, summarise, predict and generate text, trained on books, articles and web pages; for example GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters. The two terms are often used interchangeably, though "foundation" stresses breadth and "large" stresses size.

Well-known families: OpenAI GPT and o-series, DeepSeek V3/R1, Alibaba Qwen, Meta Llama, Anthropic Claude, Mistral, Google PaLM 2 and Gemini (multimodal), xAI Grok, Baidu ERNIE, TII Falcon. Versions change quickly; the engineering skills do not.

AI (generative AI) engineer skills: solid software engineering; Python, SQL and backend languages; CI/CD; Git/GitHub; LLMs and Transformers; RAG; prompt engineering; foundation models; fine-tuning; the Model Context Protocol. Job descriptions for AI/ML engineers ask for the same blend: software engineering first, ML second.

sections.title: Software engineering vs machine learning
sections.plain: SE has precise specifications; ML has examples and acceptable error rates.
sections.body:
Specification. In software engineering we can write a precise contract:

def compute_deductions(agi, expenses):
    """Returns the deductions to apply to adjusted gross income:
       capped medical expenses, 2% of AGI for charity, ..."""

For an ML function there is no such contract:

def detect_objects(image):
    """Returns the objects in the image ... ???"""

We cannot write down what every pixel pattern means; we can only give examples and say how often the function may be wrong. That gap drives everything from requirements (Session M3) to testing (Session M11).

AspectSoftware engineeringMachine learning
ApproachStructured, process-orientedData-focused
MethodologyAgile, waterfall etc. guide the life cycleRelies heavily on data; preprocessing is crucial
Nature of workDeterministic logic; predefined stagesProbabilistic models; experimental, iterative training and refinement
FocusSystem design and development processesAlgorithms (supervised, unsupervised) for pattern recognition
EvaluationFunctional correctnessAccuracy (and other statistical metrics) of the model

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• "ML replaces software engineering." It adds to it: the model still needs APIs, data pipelines, tests, deployment and monitoring.
  • "The data scientist's notebook is the product." The notebook is a prototype; the product is a maintained service.
  • "Generation 3 means no engineering." Calling a model API removes training, not integration, evaluation, cost control, privacy or monitoring.
  • "A specification is impossible for ML, so skip requirements." We specify differently: with goals, metrics, acceptable error rates and data requirements.

Code example ex1 shows the specification gap numerically: on synthetic loan data with a diagonal trade-off between income and credit score, a hand-written threshold rule reaches 71.7% test accuracy, while a learned logistic regression reaches 90.8% and discovers that ₹1,000 of monthly income is worth about 3.3 credit-score points (the true ratio used to generate the data is 0.06/0.018 ≈ 3.3).

code.title: Writing the rule vs learning the rule
code.explain: Generates synthetic loan applicants, compares a hand-written approve_loan() rule with a logistic regression learned from data, and shows the learned income/credit-score trade-off.
mistakes: Evaluating on the training data (always hold out a test set).
Assuming a learned model is always better: with little or very noisy data a clear hand-written rule may be safer and easier to audit.
code.notes: In production the learned rule lives in the model artifact; it must be versioned and monitored like code.
code.code:
# Writing the rule (software engineering) vs learning it from data (machine learning)
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 2000
income = rng.uniform(10, 90, n)            # monthly income, thousands
score = rng.uniform(400, 850, n)           # credit score
z = 0.06 * (income - 42) + 0.018 * (score - 640)
repaid = (z + rng.normal(0, 0.8, n) > 0).astype(int)   # hidden true pattern + noise

def approve_loan(income, score):
    """Hand-written specification: approve when income >= 50 and score >= 600."""
    return ((income >= 50) & (score >= 600)).astype(int)

X = np.column_stack([income, score])
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, repaid, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
rule_acc = (approve_loan(X_te[:, 0], X_te[:, 1]) == y_te).mean()

model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_tr, y_tr)   # the rule is learned, not written
ml_acc = model.score(X_te, y_te)
print(f"hand-written rule accuracy : {rule_acc:.3f}")
print(f"learned model accuracy     : {ml_acc:.3f}")
w = model.coef_[0]
print(f"learned trade-off: 1 thousand of income is worth {w[0] / w[1]:.1f} credit-score points")
new_customer = np.array([[45, 760]])
print("rule says:", approve_loan(new_customer[:, 0], new_customer[:, 1])[0],
      "| model says:", model.predict(new_customer)[0],
      f"(p = {model.predict_proba(new_customer)[0, 1]:.2f})")

hand-written rule accuracy : 0.717
learned model accuracy     : 0.908
learned trade-off: 1 thousand of income is worth 3.3 credit-score points
rule says: 0 | model says: 1 (p = 0.99)

code.title: Versioning code, data and model together
code.explain: Trains a tree under four scenarios (baseline, data changed, model changed, code changed) and fingerprints each run's code version, data snapshot and model settings, showing that a run is reproducible only when all three are recorded.
mistakes: Versioning only the code (the commonest reproducibility failure).
Forgetting random seeds, which makes the same inputs give different models.
code.notes: Tools such as Git (code), DVC (data) and MLflow (models, runs) do this at scale; see Session M6 and M14.
code.code:
# Why ML systems need versioning of code, data AND model: a tiny reproducibility ledger
import hashlib, json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

def fingerprint(obj):
    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:10]

def train(data_seed, max_depth, code_version):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(data_seed)
    X = rng.normal(size=(300, 3)); y = (X[:, 0] + 0.5 * X[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)
    m = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=max_depth, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
    Xt = np.random.default_rng(99).normal(size=(500, 3)); yt = (Xt[:, 0] + 0.5 * Xt[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)
    record = {"code": code_version, "data": f"snapshot-{data_seed}", "model": {"algo": "tree", "max_depth": max_depth}}
    return record, round(m.score(Xt, yt), 3)

ledger = []
for change, args in [("baseline", (1, 3, "v1.0")), ("data changed", (2, 3, "v1.0")),
                     ("model changed", (1, 6, "v1.0")), ("code changed", (1, 3, "v1.1"))]:
    rec, acc = train(*args)
    ledger.append((change, fingerprint(rec), acc))
for change, fp, acc in ledger:
    print(f"{change:14s} run-id {fp}  test accuracy {acc}")
again = fingerprint(train(1, 3, "v1.0")[0])
print("re-running the baseline gives the same run-id:", again == ledger[0][1])

data changed   run-id aefbf2dca2  test accuracy 0.928
model changed  run-id b26a73b881  test accuracy 0.926
code changed   run-id 3c23dcc9bb  test accuracy 0.902
